en.title: Weird story: A bamboo grows in a pot, click, click, click.
en.summary: He is very fond of weird things, and talks about nonsense, ghost things, and new things related to games every day. Kill all Starscream! (Picture/Ronaldo) I can’t be called a loyal player of business simulation games, but there are usually a lot of plants planted in such games. Generally speaking, the gameplay in simulation management and plant-related games is to plant vegetables, flowers, and trees, water them on time, and wait a few days, and a batch of neat things will grow in the ground. In reality, I also like plants. But I don’t like planting flowers that much. This is because I can’t stand a plant that doesn’t grow well for more than half a year, just to wait for a short flowering period. In comparison, buying fresh cut flowers is much easier. I also prefer to spend dozens of dollars to buy a few bunches of peonies, put them in a vase, and watch them bloom into their most beautiful flowers within a few days, and then throw them away. Water lilies are also beautiful, but none of the water lilies I bought in recent times have bloomed. I’m not sure what’s wrong, but fresh cut flowers always give me a sense of joy.

en.title: How do independent developers settle accounts when they run exhibitions?
en.summary: At the just-concluded ChinaJoy, the surrounding exhibition halls, restaurants, and cafes were crowded with developers wearing badges. Some of them look professionally dressed and serious, while others look just like tourists. During the summer, this kind of scene happens constantly in major cities. Accommodating these many works and people, there are not only large exhibitions such as Bilibili World and Firefly, but also many small exhibitions such as "Travel Opportunity" and "Development Core". But actually participating in an exhibition is always more complicated than it seems. Once, I was chatting with a publisher at a large exhibition. I pointed to their booth where players were crowded and asked, "How much does it cost to set up these?" The other party smiled and quoted 6 figures. Of course, independent game developers do not need to invest 100,000-level funds in a game exhibition, but there are still costs to bring their works to game exhibitions. en.title: One roundtable, four arenas: TapTap’s “Xia Xin Dao” martial arts game roundtable exchange meeting
en.summary: On July 31st in Shanghai, TapTap’s “Xia Xin Lun Dao” martial arts game roundtable exchange meeting was held. Wu Di from "Easy Sword", San Huang from "The Hidden Sword", Courier from "Spirit Beasts", and Hula from "Unknown Jianghu", they have brought four martial arts games with different styles. This roundtable chat lasted for nearly three hours. After the roundtable ended, I was thinking, as a classic game theme, what does martial arts games still mean today in 2026? The answer may lie in what these producers say. “A Chivalrous Heart Discussing the Tao” ■ The Stolen Sword When talking about martial arts enlightenment, the four producers had many stories to share. Although their methods of getting into martial arts are not exactly the same, they all have the same points - Jin Yong, TVB martial arts dramas, and several old games. Wu Di was born in 1986. Martial arts movies and TV series were very popular at that time. "When I was a kid, I would go downstairs to fight with other kids after watching it." Hula said that what impressed him most about martial arts was "doing something even though you know you can't do it."
